current_activity: division command post at Ennery, Moselle, in the SHAEF-reserve and Third Army area
notes: Event date: 14 January 1945 (CMH ETO-OB lists the 9th Armored Division command post at Ennery, Moselle, on 14 January). Event definition: a CMH list places the division headquarters at Ennery; the CMH table has the division assigned to Fifteenth Army and attached to Third Army from 8-9 January. Relationship: Third Army attached (from 9 Jan 45 to 21 Feb 45, CMH table); Fifteenth Army assigned (from 8 Jan 45 to 21 Feb 45, CMH table); 12th Army Group assigned (from 28 Aug 44, CMH table). The table entries start on the first row of the unbroken run (convention V-013). Location: Ennery (CMH ETO-OB command-post list, R517 p. 503: listed 14 January 1945); the town centre stands for the command post. Coordinates: Wikipedia (en): Ennery, Moselle. Event support: moderate (one official table). Location support: moderate (command post listed on the date).

current_activity: a task force reaches the Ludendorff Bridge at Remagen about 1600 and the Americans take it before demolition
notes: Event date: 7 March 1945 (Last Offensive ch. 11 p. 212-216: Task Force Engeman of the 9th Armored Division's Combat Command B, 27th Armored Infantry Battalion and 14th Tank Battalion, started at 0820 and its tanks neared the bridge at about 1600; the Combat Command was commanded by Brig. Gen. William M. Hoge). Event definition: the division takes the Ludendorff Bridge over the Rhine, the first Rhine crossing in American hands; the combat command is not a unit of the table, so the claim is the division's. Relationship: III Corps unspecified_subordination (from 22 Feb 45 to 20 Mar 45, CMH table); First Army assigned (from 22 Feb 45, CMH table); 12th Army Group assigned (from 28 Aug 44, CMH table). The table entries start on the first row of the unbroken run (convention V-013). The CMH table has a single corps column and does not say assigned or attached for a corps. Location: the Ludendorff Bridge at Remagen. Coordinates: Wikipedia (en): Ludendorff Bridge. Event support: high (Green Book and an independent Wikipedia article agree on the date and the unit). Location support: high (named bridge).

current_activity: Combat Command R of the division, with the 69th Division's 273d Infantry, takes Colditz and its prisoners
notes: Event date: 16 April 1945 (Last Offensive ch. 17 p. 393: two days after breaking free of the flak belt CCR dashed to the Mulde twenty miles southeast of Leipzig; "Having seized two bridges intact, CCR the next day, 16 April, crossed, captured Colditz, and released 1,800 Allied prisoners of war, including several ranking British officers"). Event definition: the division's reserve combat command takes the town; the release of the prisoners is recorded only as the reason the position matters. Relationship: V Corps unspecified_subordination (from 21 Mar 45 to 27 Apr 45, CMH table); First Army assigned (from 22 Feb 45 to 5 May 45, CMH table); 12th Army Group assigned (from 28 Aug 44, CMH table). The table entries start on the first row of the unbroken run (convention V-013). The CMH table has a single corps column and does not say assigned or attached for a corps. The earlier assigned relation to First Army (CR0448) is closed at 5 May 1945 (assignment_table); see the Review note on it. Location: Colditz, on the Mulde. Coordinates: Wikipedia (en): Colditz. Event support: moderate (one Green Book passage; the 273d Infantry history gives the same day and adds the infantry battalion). Location support: moderate (named town, on the date). Review (27 October 2026, found while checking this row against a source not used to write it): the regimental history of the 273d Infantry (R584) has the 3d Battalion, 273d Infantry (69th Division), as part of Combat Command R, attack Colditz on the evening of 15 April and seize the town at 1100 on 16 April after the German defenders withdrew in the night; the Green Book credits "CCR" alone, and the 9th Armored Division's self-propelled artillery supported the attack. The row is kept for the 9th Armored Division and its activity now names the infantry battalion; no row is made for the 69th Division at Colditz. Confidence stays 0.7: the second source is a unit history, not an independent official one.
